utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case IT-03-69-T, the Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber would like to deal with a few preliminaries before we continue to hear the evidence of the witness and may even be the case that we have to deal with a few even later today. The first one. The Chamber was notified by an informal communication last night at close to 7.00 p.m. that the Simatovic Defence will not be calling Witness DFS-015, but we were not informed about the availability of Witness DFS-016, who is next in line. Mr. Bakrac, once we've finished with the present witness, what are your plans?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm expecting news from the ground about the next witness who can come. They will tell me when he will come. With your leave, I would like to inform you about that before the end of today's hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but would that witness be available, well, let's say tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't think so. Not only do I not think so, I'm sure that he will not be available tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because the cancelling of the previous witness, of course, comes a bit a surprise to us, and apparently you have not taken any measures in that context to fill in the gap that now exists.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, according to our estimate made yesterday, we decided to give up on the witness that was envisaged and since then I, this morning and the rest of the day, we will try and see who will be our next witness who could be made available to the Trial Chamber as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, still it's difficult for the Chamber to understand that the day before the testimony starts you suddenly conclude that you don't want to call the witness at all. That is -- that sounds as if everything is badly prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, we are in the process of carrying out the final proofing, and so far the final proofing will lead us to our final conclusion. We were not in a position to envisage things, and as a result of our final proofing our conclusion will be that we will give up on the witness that we meant to call. We have already stated that the -- our Defence has -- is facing a lot of difficulties with regard to everything that I have already mentioned and with regard to the fact that we joined the case later, our request to be provided with more time for preparations. We are now in a position that we already indicated to the Trial Chamber. We are now in the process of finalising our list of witnesses that we will call up. All of the problems that we are facing in view of the situation that I have already described for the benefit of the Trial Chamber and which I don't want to go over again have put us in this situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it's wise not to go over it again, but it seems -- it sounds as if you say -- you gave a wrong decision. You see here are the consequences instead of adapting your work to the what the decision is, because if the Chamber decides on -- on time for preparation and if you halfway say, Of course we couldn't do that, look -- look how -- now it becomes clear to you what our problems are. That sounds as if you have not understood what a decision by the Chamber means; that is, that you have to speed up, find a solution, whatever you want to do but not to confront us a couple of hours before the start of the testimony of a witness and saying that in final proofing that it turned out that you would not call him. That is a matter which in my experience is not under normal circumstances to be expected in final proofing but should become clear already at earlier stages. Let's not talk about it any further. You have no witness ready for the remainder of the week. If you have considered it even a possibility that you would have to withdraw that witness, then you should have prepared for an alternative scenario as well, which again you apparently have not done. Let's move on with scheduling issues. Mr. Jordash, on the 22nd of February, you told us that you would contact Witness DSD-067 and DSD-061, the two -- the expert Mr. Brown and the witness Sir Roberts. On the 23rd of February we have been informed through an informal communication that Mr. Brown indicated that he would prefer to start his testimony in the week beginning the 19th of March, and we learned on the 24th of February that Sir Roberts was -- Sir Ivor was available to testify on the 26th and the 27th of March, although he preferred the 26th of March. Now, 26 of March, first of all, is a Monday, as you are aware of, and usually we are not sitting on Mondays but we could, of course, try to accommodate, but what we would very much like to have is the time estimates for the examination-in-chief and the cross-examination of both Mr. Brown and the witness so that we can try to fit it all in.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think Mr. Brown direct examination up to two hours, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Brown, two hours. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And Sir Ivor, up to an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I hear from the Simatovic Defence how much time they would need to cross-examine Mr. Brown and Sir Ivor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't think we will need more than half an hour for each of the two witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes. Good afternoon, Your Honour. I estimate that we would need two and a half hours for Mr. Brown and one and a half hours for Sir Ivor Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which means that it should be possible to hear the evidence of Sir Ivor Roberts in -- perhaps not in one day but in one day plus a little bit. We'll then consider whether we can reschedule our hearings in March to start on the Monday the 26th rather than on the 27th. I also do understand that the 19th of March, the week of the 19th of March, that would be -- we could conclude his testimony in that week relatively easily. We'll try to schedule it in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any further questions as far as scheduling is concerned? You said later today, Mr. Bakrac, you'd inform us about the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does the scheduling of Mr. Brown and Sir Ivor Roberts in any way affect your further plans as far as scheduling is concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at this moment I can't say. From this point of view, I don't think that this will have any impact. As far as we are concerned, I think that the witnesses in question can be scheduled at the given times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Bakrac. Then I move on to another subject. Mr. Jordash, on the 26th of January, and I'm talking about Witness Pelevic, you have indicated -- you objected and addressed us saying that the Prosecution had violated Rule 90(H)(iii) of the Rules by putting its case to the witness in accordance with that Rule. Then on the 21st of January you stated that you did not seek an immediate ruling on your objection, but that you would may make further motions on the matter at a later time. The Chamber then instructed parties to discuss the issue among themselves to see if there were areas of possible agreement. On the 9th of February, the Chamber requested the Stanisic Defence to clarify its position, and in particular, to specify what sort of remedy you would consider appropriate if the objection remains. Mr. Jordash, you then replied that you would revert to the Court in due course, and I don't think that there was any follow-up since the 9th of February, or have I missed something?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, I don't think there has been a follow-up. Our position is -- is, I'm afraid, as uncertain as it was then in that our preferred option is to wait until the end of the evidence and then look at our various complaints and see how they all, in our view, have accumulated and then wait for the Prosecution closing brief, and at that point we'll have all the available material to be able to decide what submissions we would like to make. And we have in mind submissions, one, concerning what the Prosecution ought to be able to now rely upon in relation to particular witness evidence, what submissions they ought to make in relation to that Prosecution evidence if they haven't put that particular aspect of their case to particular witnesses. And two, the more extreme remedy of being able to suggest to the Trial Chamber that certain evidence ought to be excluded in particular instances. These are assessments which, in our respectful submission, we cannot make at this time. We don't know what the Prosecution are going to -- to say in relation to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, Mr. Jordash, once all the evidence has been presented, of course then the Prosecution should know whether any evidence is excluded. And if you say, Well, let's first see what their final brief tell us. Of course, in that final brief they would have to know whether there's any evidence which is excluded. So therefore I do understand your argument to say, Well, we first have to look testified as whole, and then we can make the necessary submissions. What I have more difficult -- more difficulties to understand is that you say, But then we'd like first to look at to what extent they do rely on certain portions of the evidence and then make an application either to exclude it or to take your -- to choose your position, because I can imagine that the Prosecution then would ask for another final brief or at least to be able allowed to file another final brief not knowing on what evidence they could -- could rely. So part of it I do understand. Part of it I have quite a difficulty in understanding. That is the timing. Perhaps you'll think about it and --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes. I mean -- yes. If I can think about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nothing is lost to think about --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Mr. Jordash, and I'm not forcing you to already start to present the results of your intellectual activity at this moment to the Chamber. Ms. Marcus, are you still thinking, or are you going to present something?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. No. It was only on this very point. When Your Honour raised this question on the 9th of February, Your Honour inquired with Mr. Jordash as to an e-mail that was sent to the Prosecution. I'd just like to note for the record that that e-mail was sent by the Defence to the Prosecution on the 31st of January and we responded the very same day. So I would just like that to be on the record that on this issue of 90(H) with respect to Witness Pelevic we presented our responses to the Stanisic Defence the same day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course it may well be, Mr. Jordash, that if you wait and at later stage seek any remedy or any relief that of course we might be in a situation that we have to consider the -- the procedure -- proceeding that moment as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I've thought about our position, and I think in this circumstance the difference between asking Your Honours not to allow the Prosecution to be able to rely upon a particular piece of evidence is tantamount to asking them -- asking Your Honours to exclude it, because what we're engaged in is -- is the following: The Prosecution may say, We want to rely upon proposition A and the witness's answer to proposition A. We may then turn around and say, Well, you ought to have put proposition B. That is the only way you can fairly rely upon proposition -- the answer to proposition A. That's the type of intellectual exercise I can see we will want to engage with and that's why I say we can't really deal with it until we hear what the Prosecution's position is going be in relation to their various proposition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But your position is clear to the Prosecution because if you say this is what you should have done, then it should be clear to them what your complaint is. Of course, we are not privy of the -- of the e-mail exchanges between the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But the difficulty is that -- that it's an impossible task at this stage given the hundreds of possible propositions the Prosecution may seek to rely upon to be able to to say what the Prosecution should have done in a particular given situation. We can give them broad areas where we say that they failed to put their case adequately, but until they pick out the minutiae of the propositions they want to rely upon, we don't know what our position will be.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour, all I can say to that is that there were three questions put to us in that e-mail. We responded. If Mr. Jordash has some other questions he'd like to put, we're happy to respond if that would assist in his coming to his own conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, it won't, unless the Prosecution are willing to specify or able to specify precisely what detail of their case they will seek to rely upon. In a case where there are hundreds if not thousands of possible positions that they may take on a particular issue or on a particular crime base at least, the standard practice of the Prosecution when being asked to specify their case is to refer us to the indictment in the pre-trial brief. We don't expect that to change at this point in time three years after the case has started. So we can engage in a process of putting to the Prosecution what we say they should specify in relation to their case, but we'll get the same answer I fear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will think about it as well. The next and for this moment the last item, on the 19th of January, Mr. Jordash, the Stanisic Defence requested the Chamber to lift the confidentiality of the parts of evidence of Mr. Dimitrijevic, which was given in the court session of the 18th of January, the day before. You have through an informal communication invited the Chamber to lift the confidentiality of a certain portion of the cross-examination and to make that public. We do not know and since it is, of course, at this moment still evidence given in private session also do not know whether we have to go into private session to hear the position of the other parties. If all parties would agree with it, then there might be no need to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour, with you leave, I'd like to have a look at it and get back to Your Honours. I will do that later today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our Defence agrees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll hear from the Prosecution and then decide whether or not to lift the confidentiality of transcript page 16164, line 8 up to and including transcript page 16174, line 23. If there is nothing else to be raised by the parties. Mr. Bakrac, you asked for another five minutes with the present witness. Could he be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Karan. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Karan, I'd like to remind you you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Bakrac will now continue for the last five minutes his examination-in-chief. Mr. Bakrac, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Before I start putting questions to Mr. Karan, we left off last week when I was showing the map CB03 to Mr. Karan and the Registry received it as EC-44, and now I would like to tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the map that was marked by the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document saved as IC-44 will receive number D752, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Karan.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: We almost finished my direct examination last week, and we were discussing a drone that was shot down. You told us, if I'm not mistaken, that some equipment was kept by -- by Lieutenant-Colonel Letic.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, lieutenant-colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: We heard testimony here that Mr. Ajdinovic fell into disfavour in late 1994 or early 1995 and was arrested by the Serbian DB in Glina, who accused him of taking precious reconnaissance equipment from a drone, sold the equipment and pocketed the money. Are these allegations true to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is absolutely not true. I was involved in this. Petar Ajdinovic was not in the RSK from 1992 onwards, and he did not have anything to do with that drone. Lieutenant-Colonel Letic was the only one who kept the equipment, and he didn't sell it. He returned it to the Pauk command on the orders of the chief of security of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Karan, sometime after Operation Storm in 1995, did Slobodan Lazarevic ask you or demand from you that you let him go from the 21st Corps?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's impossible. I have no authority to either admit or let anyone go from the service. So this is absolutely not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did he address you with a request to allow him to leave Slavonia and go to Belgrade or something like that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That never turned up in any of my contacts with him, and I didn't seen see him when I was in the 11th Corps as the chief of security in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Karan, in the natural course of things, would you go to Topusko at the time when the Pauk operation was under way?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I duty took me there, yes. I was in Topusko several times even during the Pauk operation and all the way up to Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you have direct knowledge or did you perhaps hear as the chief of security that Franko Simatovic had some premises or offices in Topusko where he spent time, worked?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never heard of anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Was the command of your brigade in Vojnic -- sorry, was the command of your corps in Vojnic?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've said before that the corps command was based in the hunting lodge called Muljava, 3 to 4 kilometres away from Vojnic, and it was just my office, the headquarters of my section, that was in Vojnic, not far from the SUP building in the so-called cultural hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Simatovic have any office at all at the headquarters of your security section in Vojnic or in the Muljava hotel at the corps command?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't have an office on my premises, and I know for sure that he didn't have an office at the corps command either, and I don't know about any other locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karan.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. This completes my direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac. Mr. Jordash. I think your indication was that you would need one hour 15 minutes approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Karan.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have on the screen please 1D4904. Please, would you have a look at this document and see if you can cast any light on it. It's a document dated the 17th of November, 1991, and I'm dealing, just to orientate yourself, with your time with the Guards Motorised Brigade in Vukovar in 1991. This is 4904. I don't know if I said 4909, but it's 4904 is what we want. Yes, we have it. Just have a read through it and when you're finished we can go to the next page, so you can read the whole document. Perhaps we can go to page 2 of the English. And perhaps 3 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the next page of the B/C/S, please. And perhaps the last page of the English.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could all unnecessary microphones please be switched off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Are you there?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you aware of this order by Major-General Biorcevic on 17th of November, 1991, ordering - amongst other things - all forces within the zone to be identified and placed under the command of the JNA? That's at number 8 of the document. Were you aware of this order?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know this order, not this one from the 12th Corps because it's the Novi Sad Corps, but we in the Guards Motorised Brigade received a similar order, of course at a lower level than the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: At number 11, Biorcevic notes that he placed Colonel Branislav Radoman from the 12th Corps command in charge of controlling the implementation of the order and providing directives for work. Did you know that gentleman and did you observe him implementing or attempting to implement this order?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This pertains to the northern part above Vukovar, an area covered by the 12th Corps. It was, in other words, the area of responsibility of the 12th Corps. I was not aware of this item 11 that Colonel Radoman Branislav was responsible for the implementation of this order, but I knew that in our area TO staffs were under the command of the JNA, and volunteer forces also had to place themselves under the command of the JNA and that their unauthorised movement had to be prevented as well as any other irregular activities by them that would disrupt the deployment of combat forces, law and order, and the functioning of the civilian and military authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The order that you in the Guards Motorised Brigade received, was that -- the similar order that you referred to, was that at the same time or a similar time as this order?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm just saying that these orders relate to the directive from the Supreme Command proclaiming an immediate threat of war. This order is, in fact, a result of that directive.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And do you know whether in your area it was implemented?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And do you have any knowledge as to whether Biorcevic also applied it to Arkan or whether the order from your zone of responsibility was applied to Arkan?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: From our area of responsibility, the execution of this order did not relate to Arkan because he was not present there. However, this order had to be complied with without further ado, because the JNA units had to be filled to full complement and be placed at full combat readiness, and they had to have a full complement of personnel, combat equipment, and everything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge as to whether Biorcevic's personal relationship with Arkan impacted upon this order for subordination?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JNA had the rule that all interpersonal relationships had to be left outside when you are doing your work. I knew even before that they -- that they were friends, but there was no alternative but place all of them including Arkan and his volunteers under the JNA command.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And do you know that as a fact, did you observe that as a fact, that Arkan was, at least following this order, placed under direct subordination to the Novi Sad Corps vis-a-vis this order?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a fact. All forces were to be placed under the command of the highest-ranking unit in the field. No alternative to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Karan, I'm not dispute what you're say, but I'm trying to ascertain the source of your knowledge. Were you told that? Did you see it yourself in military operations? How do you know this to be a fact in relation to Arkan?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know because I know how the volunteers who were in the operation group south were treated. There's no reason why it should be any different with the operation group north. There was no improvisation there. It was a fact that was obvious on the ground, and it's an absolute truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Let me have you look at something else which is related. 1D03611, please, on the screen, and it's -- what you're going to be shown, Mr. Karan, is a section of minutes from the 27th session of the Supreme Defence Council of the FRY, and if we could orientate ourselves by looking at page 1 in the first instance so you can see who attended this particular session. We can see there amongst the attendees there's Milosevic, Lilic, Perisic, and others. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And if we can go to page 10 of the English -- sorry, page 11 of the English and 11 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. According to our information, parts of these minutes are under -- should be under seal. I have certain pages indicated. I can provide that information to Mr. Jordash if he wants, but I think out of an abundance of caution this should not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I don't recall a -- I mean, I recall a lengthy discussion about whether they should be, and I recall alerting the Chamber to the fact that had appeared on a public and do appear on a public web site, but if that's the Prosecution's cautious position, I'm happy to follow that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is quite a large body of evidence. Obviously the SDC minutes, there was a lot of debate about it. We have very detailed charts that have been put together as to which pieces of which SDC minutes, et cetera, so in an abundance of caution as I said I think that we should probably be discreet about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not to be shown to the public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Portions were already shown to the public. Ms. Marcus, is there anyway for you to find out whether those portions are affected by -- you have, you said, all kind of charts, and unfortunately the Chamber has not. Could someone try to find out, because otherwise we would have to make a video redaction.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: According to the information I have, page 1 and page 10 are among those to which protective measures apply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then a video redaction is hereby ordered. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, the -- thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, the subject I want to deal with now is Bora Ivanovic, and I'd like you to read page 11 and moving through to page 16, please, and I want to ask you about what you know, if anything, about the prosecution of Ivanovic for co-operating with the likes of Arkan.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know if General Ivanovic was ever prosecuted for the friendly and good relations he had with Arkan, but I know the man myself, and I know that he was not quite an honourable officer, that he was involved in some activities that are not appropriate to the rank of officer, activities that are criminal in nature, and he was also bent on some irregularities outside the service, like drunkenness, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you for the answer. Let me try to shortcut things, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If we can go to page 14 of the English and 15 of the B/C/S -- sorry, 14 of both, and Perisic there is -- is -- there's a discussion about Ivanovic, and Perisic notes: "The commission came to a conclusion, that is, going to the court and the court will prove that Bora a gave 4 million bullets contrary to your order." "Milosevic: When did he give them?" Perhaps if I'm going to read we should go into private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And what I'm interested in is the message sent by Perisic according to Mladic that in August of 1994, Milosevic wanted Mladic or was urging him to refuse obedience to the RS leadership, which according to the message is leading the people into disaster, and I read halfway down the English page: "He wants you to make a U-turn in policy that the plan can be accepted." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And then if we go over to page 283 of the English and B/C/S, we see Mladic's view of that proposal, and two-thirds of the way down the English: "What is asked of us is to refuse obedience to the RS leadership - that is an immature idea, which is the same as if the VJ was asked to refuse obedience to the FRY leadership. "Milosevic's statement that the RS leadership has separated from the Serbian interests must not be a cause for discord in the army." Were you aware of the depth of Milosevic's frustration with the RS leadership and his attempt to encourage Mladic to rebel?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we knew a lot about the functioning of the political power and the functioning of the military. Similar things happened in our midst. The political authorities were not concerned with the overall interest, and that particularly reflected in the Republic of Serbian Krajina. At least in Republika Srpska it functioned in a way, much better than in our midst. It was only in 1994 that there were some attempts here to have political authorities functioning. The interest of particular political leaders were totally different. There was a group in favour of total integration in Croatia, and the others were completely against that. In the Republika Srpska, everybody was aware of the fact how that Mladic had a negative attitude towards Karadzic. They were not on good terms. They clashed constantly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, in August of 1994, where were you based and what were your day-to-day tasks?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In August of 1994, I was chief of security of the 21st Corps. We were engaged in very serious activities, i.e., combat activities. We were engaged against the 5th Corps of the BiH Army and the popular defence of Western Bosnia. In mid-August we received a lot of refugees, and all of the troops of the popular defence of Western Bosnia. They all arrived in our territory. That took up a lot of our time. We organised their accommodation. We're talking about some 50.000 or 60.000 refugees who were accommodated in Turinje and Batnoga camps. We also had smaller groups of refugees roaming about. We would collect them, and we would steer them towards the camps. People were fleeing combat activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May we take a break, Your Honour, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We take a break, and we resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm going to return to your precise role in a moment, Mr. Karan, but you've raised the issue of 50- to 60.000 refugees, and I want to deal with Fikret Abdic's meetings with you and what you know about Fikret Abdic's motivations.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have on the screen, please, 1D05440.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What's coming on the screen is a letter that Fikret Abdic apparently sent to Bill Clinton, who was then the President of the US. Just have a quick flick through it. It's dated, as you'll see at the end, the 7th of October, 1994, so just before Pauk began. Now, let's -- because we're short of time, let's turn to page 3 of the English and page 2 of the B/C/S, and there Abdic, at the bottom of -- or towards the bottom of page 3 of the English, notes: "People of Western Bosnia were the first ones to reject such insane intentions and with its exodus it drew the attention to the future cataclysms which are yet to come. Sixty thousand people who fled in front of terror will soon reach Europe, as well, is proud of its historical resistance." And: "Regardless of the torture of representatives of international organisations which deprive us of the right to live, food, water, accommodation, medications, trying to force us to go back to the private state of Alija Izetbegovic, we will endure in our sacrifice." And then turning to the page 3 of the B/C/S and page 4 of the English. Towards the bottom of page 4: "The thing which needs to be done urgently is to provide enough supplies, accommodation, and health care for more than 60.000 refugees." Now, Mr. Karan, you were -- were you seeing Fikret Abdic on a regular basis at this point in time, and, if so, does that reflect his view, and did that reflect the situation on the ground?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. I met with Fikret several times a week. We had to implement some activities together in order to organise the life of the people in every sense of the word. It was our obligation to organise the militarily able-bodies refugees. We didn't want them to scatter all over the territory of Kordun. I know for a fact that this was Fikret Abdic's position towards the authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina and in particular towards Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if you wish me to say anything else. I don't know what your question was, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You answered part of it. In relation to the 60.000 refugees, in October of 1994, before the beginning of Pauk, what was the general condition of these refugees? Were they suffering from a lack of basic food supplies and so on?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were not exactly starving, but there were problems with health care. We had some people who were sick. We had problems with very young children. The capacity of our hospital in Vojnici in Kordun could not meet the demand of so many people. Moreover, we had to reorganise our own forces to engage with the 5th Corps. We had to deploy our troops along the length of the border with Western Bosnia. The situation was dire but not unsustainable.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I tender this document as an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we've objected before to these documents, I believe, because they come from Mr. Stanisic's own personal collection.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The witness has authenticated the facts within the document, and there's no reason to suspect that this document isn't authenticate reflecting as it does the views expressed by Fikret Abdic at the time, whether they came from the accused or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness has agreed with a portion of the document, that is true, but there's quite a lot in the document, and I don't know why the Defence can't get the -- the original version. What we -- we -- as a -- as a matter of principle, we -- we oppose documents that come from the collection of the accused. So that's our position, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I leave it in Your Honours' hands. They come from the accused. There's no reason to suspect on the face of it that this is anything other than an authentic document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Under normal circumstances one would ask the provider of document where he got it from, et cetera, et cetera, and of course Mr. Stanisic is not taking the stand as a witness. It will marked for identification. We'll consider the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If we can provide that information of course, then we will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If that would, of course, then convince Ms. Marcus. That's a -- it's an indirect way of receiving information which may be relevant to our decision whether or not we'll admit. Now, there's one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we ask Madam Registrar to provide a number, the original - which is most likely not the original - have you inspected that, Ms. Marcus? I mean the copy in terms of whether it's -- sometimes you can see whether it's a scanned document. Sometimes you can see -- and I may have missed questions in relation to the signature. Mr. Jordash, forgive me when I have not been attentive enough, but did you ask whether the witness recognises the signature as the one of Fikret Abdic, or have you --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- compared it with any other --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I'd -- perhaps that can be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- known signatures of Fikret Abdic? Perhaps that --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, that might help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- might be the -- might help, yes. Perhaps a comparison as well. Perhaps you could ask the witness. It's on your screen at this moment. Can you -- you see those -- on this copy there's a signature. Do you recognise that signature? I could ask you whether you recognise this, the one of Fikret Abdic, because to leave that as an open question is, of course, where the name Fikret Abdic has been mentioned now ten times and his name appears just above it. But do you recognise what you see on this letter as being the -- as being similar to the signature of Fikret Abdic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is quite. I know it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that the original is somewhere in the US archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We have the original. Mr. Stanisic received it from Fikret Abdic's Chief of Cabinet, a man called Arif Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Or Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, I take it that the real original has been sent to the addressee.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you have another copy. That's what you --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: That's what I meant, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- wanted to say but which comes close. You have that. Ms. Marcus, perhaps it -- despite the fact that you, in general terms, oppose to documents coming from the accused, of course if there are serious doubts, there are other ways of verifying the authenticity of the letter, but the first step, I would think, is to inspect the one -- the copy which is in the hands of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think upon looking at that I can give our final position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then the -- Madam Registrar, the number of this letter would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D5440 will receive number D755, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D755 is marked for identification. You may proceed Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Similarly, could we have a look at 1D05441 which is a letter from Fikret Abdic, dated again the 7th of October. I'm not going to dwell on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'll just ask you to look at the signature and see if you recognise it in the first instance. If we can go to page 2 of the B/C/S and 3 of the English. Do you recognise the signature, Mr. Karan?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. That's his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And go -- if we can go back to page 1. This is a letter to Ms. Ogata. Are you able to confirm Ms. Ogata was the commissioner for refugees for the UN at the time?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's general knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I tender this exhibit -- as an exhibit as well, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The same procedure, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D5441 will receive number D756, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D756 is marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do -- do -- sorry, let me start that again. Did you speak to Fikret Abdic about the Pauk operation and about the agreement with Milosevic that Serbia would try to assist with the situation on the ground in and around November of 1994?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, except that Fikret Abdic did not call it Operation Pauk. Instead, he said that he must, at all costs, for the sake of the people of the Autonomous Region of Western Bosnia, return to his territory. There were quite a few such contacts, especially because he derived optimism from his talks with President Milosevic who had told him that all assistance would be provided to make his idea come true, and in this connection the command of our corps also reorganised its forces and established a so-called ready unit of battalion strength, around 500 men, carefully selected men between 25 and 35 from all infantry brigades with different arms also attached to them such as armoured units, artillery support, part of logistical support and such.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: As far as Abdic was concerned, the agreement that had been reached with Milosevic and Karadzic was the help that he'd been seeking for many a month before from different parties, from the UN, from Bill Clinton, and so on, this for Fikret Abdic was welcome assistance, no?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're perfectly right. It was a matter of life and death.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Why do you say a matter of life and death? Why do you put it in that way?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because his idea was that he has, absolutely has to go back. He did not accept what happened in August as a military defeat. In addition to the attack of the 5th Corps, I think it was also a political operation to make people think twice about the policy of Fikret Abdic and his idea to create Bosnia as he envisioned it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I see a mistake in the transcript in line 16. A different name is written than the one the witness pronounced, which changes the meaning of the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll read to you part of the transcript. Witness, it reads now: "I think it was also a political operation to make people think twice about the policy of..." And what name did you then mention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To think twice or think again about the fate of the people of Western Bosnia and the policies of Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That also sounds more logical. So about the policy of Alija Izetbegovic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And do you know why Fikret Abdic -- I don't want to dwell on any -- the obvious, but do you know why Fikret Abdic saw it as so critical to return to the Bihac pocket?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fikret Abdic was the leader of the people in that region. People believed in him, and he could not betray them. Only someone who was in the area of Kordun when those people fled knows how much authority he wielded among the masses despite the fact that they lived very poorly. He was an unrivalled leader in that region, and although he's now in prison in Rijeka, I believe there is still a political division in Velika Kladusa between those are in favour of Fikret and those who are against him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And it's correct, isn't it, that Abdic had previously won the presidential elections against Izetbegovic but had given up that post; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. He was the absolute winner at the multi-party elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina as a candidate running for the SDA. However, for various reasons, he refused to become president of the Presidency, and he accepted only to be the leader of his own people in the territory of Velika Kladusa municipality and an area perhaps slightly broader than that. He did not subscribe to the Islamic Declaration by Alija Izetbegovic. He was a man of peace, a leader of industry, commerce, production, and he was certainly not in favour of war. He was practically pushed into resisting the 5th Corps' operation by the commander of the 5th Corps, Ramiz Durakovic, who was an extremist who mistreated the people of Western Bosnia through his military and police structures, and that's how it began. That's how the conflict and the rift among the people began.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And it's correct, isn't it, that Fikret Abdic didn't have any territorial ambitions beyond controlling an area and avoiding that area being dragged into any conflict that was raging within Bosnia? Do I summarise that fairly?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have on the screen, please, 1D02454.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm going to stay with the same subject of the run-up to Pauk, and it's a State Security Department document dated the 11th of October, 1994, entitled: "The Cazin Krajina - Information About Forces of the So-Called Government of the BiH (5th Corps)." And if you just have a quick look through it, you'll see the document describing the military preparedness of the 5th Corps in October of 1994. And I'm particularly interested if we can turn to page 3 of the English and page 2 of the B/C/S. We see a general discussion being completed about the operation Tiger and Sloboda '94. It's a 5th Corps operation which seized the entire territory of the Cazin Krajina. And the bit I'm interested in is where the issue of the Serbian support is discussed. The top of page 3 in the English. "In the conflicts between Fikret Abdic and the 5th Corps, the Serbian side supported Abdic (by supplying him with weapons and ammunition, providing artillery support, et cetera). Both the VRSK and the VRS were involved in providing the support (but we do not know how co-ordinated it was). For the most part, the Serbs were employing cautious tactics while supporting Fikret Abdic which was aimed at maintaining the status quo and having the two Muslim sides exhaust each other because the assessment was that Abdic was closer to the Croatian than the Serbian side." And now my question is: This State Security Department 2nd Administration report, dated the 11th of October, 1994, assesses that Abdic is receiving support with weapons and ammunition from two sources connected to the Serbian side, the VRSK and the VRS. Do you agree that that was the support Abdic was receiving up until October of 1994, from those two separate sources?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's absolutely true. With the proviso that the Army of Republika Srpska did not provide materiel and equipment to the army of Fikret Abdic. Our side did that, the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. The VRS had co-ordinated operations with his army against the forces of the 5th Corps. There were many problems in agreeing about combat operations and offensives for all sorts of reasons. Usually it was mistakes made by the army of the national defence of Western Bosnia. They would be late or they would fail to follow the axes envisaged by the plan of operation, et cetera. They were not organised well enough, certainly worse than the VRS or the VRSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Right. Now, let me ask you this: As far as you're concerned through your work within the security organ as you've described to us in 1994, at this point in time you're not aware of any supplies coming directly to Serbia to assist Fikret Abdic. Am I correct about that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Assistance to Fikret Abdic by equipment and ammunition, that was mainly conducted by secret depots of the VRSK. Later, however, he could only be supplied from the territory of the FRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: When was later? What do you put that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the establishment of the Pauk command and the development of the plan of co-ordinated combat operations against the 5th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The secret depots of the VRSK. Where were they and how well supplied were they?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I say "secret depots," they were not secret to us. They were secret to the UNPROFOR command of the Sector North after the decision that heavy weaponry and artillery must be placed 20 kilometres away from the border of Croatia and 20 kilometres away from the border of the national defence of Western Bosnia army. They were placed in private cellars, basements, family houses, et cetera, yards.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Was there a large warehouse in Cerkezevac, C-e-r-k-e-z-e-v-a-c, near Kladusa?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We, the 85th Logistics Base had a big depot, and there have another big depot at Petrova Gora in a facility called Spomenik. You cited the name correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And was there one in Dosnica in Golubic?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At Golubic there was a depot of strategic reserves. In addition to lethal ammunition, there was also fuel. I did not understand the second place name. I didn't understand your pronunciation at least, or perhaps I don't know that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Dosnica. D-o-s-n-i-c-a. I think we're talking, I suspect, about the same place. Dosnica which is or was in Golubic?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a sector around Golubic, but Golubic was the name of this depot of strategic reserves.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I see. And how plentiful were the supplies in 1994 pre-Pauk? Was Fikret Abdic able to receive all the supplies he required to assist him with his operations pre-Pauk?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've said earlier that Fikret Abdic never received all the equipment he requested, partly because the command and the political structures did not fully trust him. And when I say "command," I mean some in the command who believed that if he is given all the weapons that he wanted --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry to cut you off. Let me be just a bit more specific. What I'm after is a description of how plentiful the supplies were. Whether if the political or military will had been there, could the SVK in your view have supplied Fikret Abdic with all his requests?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a limited operation, yes, but to support him fully, I don't think they would have been able to.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your last question is of some concern to me. You say, "I'm after a description of how plentiful the supplies were." And you added then, "If the political or military will had been there, could the SVK in your view have supplied Fikret Abdic with all his requests." These are two matters mixed up. The one is what do you need, and the second is is there sufficient material to supply. Plentifulness includes both elements which are not clearly separated in your question, so I'm a bit confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You've answered, Mr. Karan, that for a limited operation the SVK could have supported Fikret Abdic fully; correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But then you seem to suggest that for something other than a limited operation there wouldn't -- or the SVK would not have been able to provide him fully. Am I understanding you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And was that because the warehouses just didn't contain enough supplies or the SVK itself didn't have the supplies to give?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. We in the corps command made assessments of our supplies, and we could not provide them with everything, because we didn't have enough, plus the war with Croatia was in the offing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Hence -- no, I'll leave it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No more questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karan.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Jordash. Ms. Marcus, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Karan, you'll now be cross-examined by Ms. Marcus. Ms. Marcus is counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Karan.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: An Operational Group is a temporary formation with different units performing a certain task within a given time period under a temporary unity of command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could interpret it that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: For the purposes of the Vukovar operation, the JNA were the dominant forces. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And the Guards Brigade was renamed by the fact that some other units were attached to it and then it was called OG South; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The Guards Motorised Brigade was never renamed. It's just that the commander of the Guards Motorised Brigade was appointed commander of the Operation Group south.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Karan, those were in fact your words in the Mrksic case that I just put to you, so perhaps let me ask my question with my words. The Guards Brigade, combined with some other units, were combined and then -- combined under the command of OG South. Would you agree with that then?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree with that and with what I said a little while ago. The Guards Brigade didn't lose its name. It continued to exist. In OG South there were other units, and besides the security organs there was another unit in charge of -- of that unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: You told us on the 22nd of February, at transcript page 17672, that in the context of the Vukovar operation, "the Territorial Defence and other structures fell under the JNA command." If I understand you correctly, although the dominant military operations were the operations of the JNA in the area where it was, units of the Territorial Defence were temporarily resubordinated to OG South during the time of your operations there in relation to Vukovar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. While the order was in place for an imminent threat of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, as the assistant for counter-intelligence for the security organ of the Guards Motorised Brigade, you also played a role in monitoring and advising and guiding OG South more generally in respect of counter-intelligence threats. In other words, your responsibilities were not restricted purely to security issues of the Guards Motorised Brigade, but you also had some security responsibilities in relation to OG South more broadly. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have no translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus, could you please have a look at the transcript and resume where we left off without interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Karan, I had just put to you a question. Perhaps you could indicate whether you recall it. I asked you -- I said your responsibilities were not strictly purely related to security issues of the Guards Motorised Brigade, but you also had some security responsibilities in relation to OG South more broadly. Could you please kindly repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can repeat my answer. Security organs of the Guards Motorised Brigade were not also the security organs of OG South. In order for them to become that, a new security organ should have been set up, but that could have been done only pursuant of a decision by the security administration. The disseminated units of the OG South had their security organs who had their chain of reporting towards their superiors, towards their superior commands, i.e., their superior security organ. It is completely erroneous to claim that the security organ of the Guards Brigade was also the security organ of OG South. That simply was not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Allow me to intervene. On line 13 and on line 14, the institution that should have issued a decision that the witness was talking about was erroneously recorded.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A decision should have been passed by the security administration of the SSNO. The Federal Secretariat of National Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I stopped talking. The witness immediately took over, and now as we read the transcript, it seems as if I was the one who talked instead of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It looks on the transcript that you told us by whom a decision should have been passed, and if I understand you well, it was the witness who told us, and I think we can then proceed. By the way, before we do so, Ms. Marcus, you referred to a quote of the witness. Let me just have a look. On the 22nd of February, and you referred us to page -- I couldn't find it on the page, and therefore I --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I intended to refer to page 17672, line --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: -- lines 5 through 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it very much looks -- because that's not on the 22nd of February. I think that the correct reference would be 17752. That's at least where it appears in my -- let me just check again.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I must confess that in the transcript that I have, as of the end of the day on the 23rd, we were only up to page 17744, and then we have today's temporary transcript. One of us must be incorrect. I'm sure it's me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, as a matter of fact, that the page I mentioned has a better chance of -- let me just check again. Yes, it is 17752, where I found it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now -- yes. We have it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Karan, on the topic that you were just talking about, there was quite a lot of debate in your previous testimony. I'm just going to focus on the part that's relevant for our discussion today. Now as part of your security role with the Guards Motorised Brigade, you would've, at a minimum, had to have been informed about the security situation regarding the other units under operational command of OG South. Would that be accurate?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you can put it that way. We exchanged information.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, since the TO was temporarily resubordinated to the JNA, you would have informed, whether formally or through an exchange of information as you say, of any security-related information in connection with the activities of those TO units who were resubordinated to OG South for the Vukovar operation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, in your capacity as assistant for counter-intelligence, your role was to follow or monitor the security situation. The aim would be, among others, to identify any activity that could endanger your unit and to suggest or undertake measures to remove that threat. In this capacity, it would have been part of your job to identify any activity carried out by the TO forces under the temporary resubordination of the JNA which could impact upon the security situation for the Guards Motorised Brigade. Would that being accurate?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partly. One could say that my colleague from the TO staff proposed measures to his superior, to his command, and those measures concerned JNA units and possibly their activities that might have threatened the command or the Motorised Brigade units. However, there were no such situations. There were no such misunderstandings on the ground, or at least I don't recall any from that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: During your testimony, and I hope I get the page right this time, Your Honour, on the 22nd of February, at transcript page 17674, you were asked: "Do you know that in the area of responsibility of the Novi Sad Corps, within the Territorial Defence there was also a group of volunteers led by Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you noted rightly a minute ago that the transcript starts at 17677, so it could not be under the 22nd of February. So it must be -- I'll find it for you if you have a little quote. I'll be able to find it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes. All I can say, sir, is that right in front of me, I'm looking from the 22nd of February, page 17674, and I find my quote there. I'm sure that I have a technical glitch or something that makes it inconsistent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is for me the -- if you please proceed, I'll try to find the quote.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I will do. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Is it possible to take a break and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you'd say it would take me a while to find that quote. We'll take a break a bit earlier than -- no. This is the usual time for the break. We'll take a break and resume at 5.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We start quite a bit later. Mr. Bakrac, at the end of this session we'll stop a bit earlier. I'll give you some more information about scheduling and that's what kept us busy during the whole of this longer break, but since the witness is in --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I'd rather take five or seven minutes of this session than deal with the matter at this moment. Yes. Mr. Jordash, may I take it that you want to tender something?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, please. 1D02454, if it could be MFI'd until we provide the Prosecution with provenance information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that is the information about forces of the so-called government of BiH, the 11th of October, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D2454 will receive number D757, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I hear of no objections. D757.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, we do object, Your Honour, based on provenance information that we're waiting for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Provenance. Therefore is marked for identification. And we'd like to hear from the parties soon. Then where the minutes were MFI'd before the break, the minutes D753, Mr. Jordash, they are MFI'd under seal. That doesn't come as a surprise, I take it. Then I further have to find out whether on my computer the transcript versions are not updated. Apparently we're working from different versions, and it might be that mine is old. Now, I usually do not do that myself, updating. We'll see what happened and at least the version which -- I said the 22nd of February, which in my version starts at 17677, starts in the version I just received a hard copy, at page 17597, which may explain some of the inconsistencies in the version I apparently was working from and you used, Ms. Marcus. I apologise for the confusion created there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Yes, just, we confirmed it with the Defence and the Registry. We all, the Prosecution, the Defence, and the Registry all have the same page numbering. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I'll have to pay specific attention to the updating of my electronic transcript. Are you ready to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so, and could you finish in approximately one hour from now so that I have a couple of minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Before I begin with respect to the 19th of January request by the Stanisic Defence to lift confidentiality of part of Dimitrijevic's evidence, we do not have any objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then all parties agree, which means that transcript pages T-16164, line 8, up to and including 16174, line 23 are -- will be public and are not confidential any more. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And with respect to D574, MFI, we received provenance information over the break, and we're satisfied it comes from an RFA, so we withdraw our objection to that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which means that nothing opposes admission any more. D574 is admitted into evidence. Any need to have it under seal ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Then it's a public exhibit. Please proceed, Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could I ask that -- we've received the originals of D755 and D756, both MFI'd from the Defence. Could I ask that they be shown to the witness so that he can look at the original signature rather than looking at it. These are the Abdic -- purported Abdic letters to President Clinton and Ms. Ogata.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I expect the originals to be somewhere in the United States, but could we then later have a look at what has been shown to the witness so that we know how original they are.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Karan, could I just ask you to look at those and especially to the signature and tell us whether you are able to confirm that that is the signature of Fikret Abdic on both?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the signature -- signature, because that's how he signed the document when he presented a pistol to me as a gift.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I withdraw our objection. They can be admitted. We would also request that those originals also be admitted physically into evidence. They are -- Your Honours, they are in coloured signature. They appear to be the original documents. So our only remaining question, then, to the Defence was: Were these letters, in fact, ever sent?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to give evidence, so I don't know the answer to that off the top of my head. That's one thing. And secondly, I can see no reason why the originals would have to be filed with the court since the copies are perfectly adequate copies and the Prosecution don't object to -- to their authenticity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we first have a look at them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus, you've asked the originals to be -- to be admitted into evidence. The question you're raising in relation to this is that this seems to be, indeed, an original typewritten letter which you would expect in the archives of the addressee rather than of anyone else, so therefore there still remain a few questions -- at least you could raise questions. Whether they remain or not depends on many things. In order to not lose - Mr. Jordash, I'm now addressing you as well - in order not to lose the opportunity to, at any later stage, to inspect the originals, at least these originals, it's -- again, it's not a -- it is not a photocopy, it is not a carbon copy, it looks as if both would then have been retyped, which is still is not impossible. I also see that they have often been stapled. The Chamber would like to instruct you to keep them in your possession and available for inspection whenever there's any need to further inspect them. Would such instruction cause you any problems, Mr. Jordash?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus works it meet your concerns?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then these copies are to be returned to the Stanisic Defence. Mr. Jordash keeps the originals, and the electronic versions of the two letters are now admitted into evidence. Madam Registrar, the numbers were -- I think Ms. Marcus mentioned them, but.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: D755 and 756, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D755 and D756 are admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and just to be clear, it's all right with Your Honour if I continue to use the transcript references that I have in my notes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Use yours. They seem to be far better than mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Karan, during your testimony on the 22nd of February, at page 17674, you were asked: "Do you know that in the area of responsibility of the Novi Sad Corps, within the Territorial Defence there was also a group of volunteers led by Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan?" Your reply was: "I learned about that when I was still a member of the security administration, because at our meetings we discussed information about him." You also said at that same page: "We already had information that Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, had placed himself under the command of the Territorial Defence, that he had a training camp, and that he had been armed by the JNA from JNA depots." There has been a suggestion in this case that Arkan's SDG was a permanent unit of the JNA in the SBWS in the fall of 1991. Does this accord with your own knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Arkan's unit was a permanent unit on the strength of the Territorial Defence that was resubordinated to the JNA. That would be a more precise way of putting it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Perhaps another way to put it would be that Arkan's SDG were at times temporarily and operationally subordinated to the JNA for the purposes of specific combat operations. Would that accord with your understanding of the situation?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One could interpret the situation in that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Were Arkan's men either in whole or in part ever temporarily resubordinated to OG South for the purposes of the Vukovar operation?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. While that operation was on, they were not active in our area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Just so that I understand your evidence correctly, at no time during the Vukovar operation, to your knowledge, were Arkan's SDG involved. Did I get that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KARAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you did not. The Vukovar operation involved actions from both north and south. I am testifying about OG South, and I'm saying that Arkan's forces did not participate in any of the OG South activities.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Okay. But they did participate in the Vukovar operation, but your evidence is that that was not under the resubordination of OG South; is that correct?
